# Education in New Zealand
Education in New Zealand has a rich history beginning with traditional Māori wānanga for transmitting tribal knowledge before formal European-style schooling was introduced in 1815 by missionaries teaching in the Māori language. The establishment of a free, compulsory, and secular national state education system commenced in 1878, largely modeled on the Canterbury system, influenced by Victorian ideals, and evolving through grammar schools and provincial education boards. Early childhood education is widely accessed, comprising center-based teacher-led services (kindergartens, Puna Reo, licensed centers) and whānau-led services (Kohanga Reo, Playcentre), all licensed by the Ministry of Education and guided by the Te Whāriki curriculum.
Primary and secondary education is free and compulsory between ages 6 and 16, with schooling lasting from Year 1 (age 5) to Year 13 (age 17). The curriculum follows national guidelines (The New Zealand Curriculum for English-medium schools or Te Marautanga o Aotearoa for Māori-medium schools) covering eight learning areas, with literacy, numeracy, and optional languages emphasized. Most students work towards the National Certificate of Educational Achievement (NCEA), with some schools offering Cambridge or International Baccalaureate qualifications. Schools include state schools (government funded and secular), state-integrated schools (maintaining a special character with attendance dues), and private schools (tuition-based). Māori language education underwent suppression in the early 20th century but has since experienced revival through bilingual and immersion initiatives such as kōhanga reo and kura kaupapa Māori. Māori-medium schools show higher achievement for Māori students relative to mainstream schools. School enrolment schemes are prevalent in urban areas, using home zones to manage capacity. Education funding for schools is government-allocated based on enrollment and socio-economic deciles; voluntary donations and attendance dues also contribute. The education system has faced challenges such as disparities in achievement, bullying, and concerns over teaching methods in numeracy, but maintains a structured, inclusive approach with growing recognition of Māori educational pathways and cultural integration.
